title: Democracy Under Stress and the Transformation of the Global Order
gist: A convergence of eroding democratic legitimacy, China's rising appeal as a development model in Latin America, AI/robotics-driven labor displacement, and a coming revolution in autonomous military affairs is transforming the global order in ways that favor authoritarian solutions and an eventual PRC overtaking of the U.S., with Taiwan as a likely flashpoint.

insights.claim: In a Latinobarometro poll, half of respondents surveyed in Latin America said they would support a leader who could deliver results even if it required adopting nondemocratic solutions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A 50% acceptance rate for authoritarian trade-offs is a leading indicator of political risk for democratic governance and policy continuity across Latin American markets.
insights.quote: half of those surveyed in Latin America said they would support a leader who could deliver results, even if it were necessary to adopt nondemocratic solutions

insights.claim: Recent elections in Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru were dominated by insecurity and governance-performance issues, with corruption fueled partly by transnational criminal activity undermining hope that democratic institutions can improve conditions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Insecurity-driven electoral volatility across multiple major Latin American economies is a recurring political-risk theme for regional investors.
insights.locator: Recent elections in Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru

insights.claim: AI and hyperconnected social media have distorted and atomized democratic discourse while making the fabrication or distortion of content commonplace, feeding public cynicism even as they expand content and information access.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Frames AI-driven information distortion as a direct structural threat to democratic institutions, not just a content-moderation nuisance.
insights.locator: AI has also greatly expanded content

themes.theme: China's surveillance-state model and its export

insights.claim: China's use of facial-recognition cameras linked to citizen financial and other data, internet controls, and public transportation has made real what philosopher Jeremy Bentham called the Panopticon, enabling levels of state control the former Soviet Union only aspired to.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Positions China's surveillance-tech stack as a more advanced and effective authoritarian control model than any historical precedent — a key comparator for assessing authoritarian resilience.
insights.locator: Nowhere is this more visible than in the People's Republic of China

insights.claim: China-derived citizen-surveillance and control architectures have been adopted by authoritarian allies, including the Fatherland ID Card in Venezuela, the ECU-911 integrated security system in Ecuador, and the BOL-110 integrated command, control, and citizen-security system in Bolivia.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Names three specific Latin American countries running Chinese-linked surveillance systems, a concrete map of China's tech-enabled political influence in the region.
insights.locator: This includes architectures in China and in authoritarian allies

insights.claim: A recently released AMLAT Radar survey shows that, for the first time, 36 percent of Latin Americans chose China as the best model for development — a 7-percentage-point increase since a 2022 survey — while those choosing the United States fell 13 percentage points, dropping the U.S. to third place behind Japan.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A first-ever flip to China as the preferred development model in Latin America is a major soft-power inflection point with implications for U.S. regional influence and trade alignment.
insights.quote: for the first time, Latin Americans see China, not the United States, as the best model for development: 36 percent of respondents chose the PRC
insights.locator: A recently released survey by AMLAT Radar

themes.theme: Six forces transforming the global order

insights.claim: The rules-based international order is unraveling at an accelerating rate, driven by a growing synergy between an increasingly powerful PRC and a disparate group of illiberal states including Iran, Venezuela, and North Korea, which offers these regimes alternatives to Western rules and helps them survive in ways that distract and undermine the United States.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Frames a coordinated (if unplanned) illiberal bloc as the structural driver of order breakdown, a key lens for assessing sanctions-evasion and multilateral-institution risk.
insights.locator: First, the rules-based international order is now unraveling

insights.claim: New technologies have given smaller states and nonstate actors unprecedented ability to disrupt much larger actors, evident in Iran's use of drones to keep the Strait of Hormuz unstable, the Houthis in the Bab-al-Mandeb strait, Ukraine's fight against Russia, and criminal organizations in Mexico and Colombia.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Technology-enabled asymmetric disruption capability is now a durable feature of global conflict, raising baseline volatility for shipping, energy, and infrastructure risk premiums.
insights.locator: Second, new technologies, in addition to bolstering the power

insights.claim: In July 2026, hackers breached the systems of Colombian state petroleum firm Ecopetrol, stealing data from more than 3,300 accounts, part of a broader pattern of criminal and nonstate cyber warfare against companies and states.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A concrete recent breach at a major state-owned oil company illustrates escalating cyber risk for critical Latin American energy infrastructure.
insights.locator: More recently, in July 2026, hackers breached the system

insights.claim: The proliferation of PRC open-source AI models such as Kimi and DeepSeek, capable of rapidly exploiting vulnerabilities in commercial and government architectures and disabling physical systems, will give small states and criminal extortionists more options to wield disruptive power.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Open-source Chinese AI models are flagged as a proliferation risk for offensive cyber capability among non-state actors, relevant to cybersecurity and critical-infrastructure defense spending.
insights.locator: The proliferation of PRC open-source AI models

insights.claim: AI-empowered robots from companies such as Tesla, Unitree, and UBTech are already deployed on factory floors, in homes, and for police patrols in the PRC, and the cost per hour of a factory robot financed over its five-year life is already less than a human factory worker's salary in most advanced countries.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Robots already undercutting human factory-labor cost is a concrete economic threshold with direct implications for manufacturing employment and automation capex cycles.
insights.quote: The cost per hour of a factory robot, financed over its five-year life, is already less than the salary of a human factory worker in most advanced countries
insights.locator: The expanding capability of AI-empowered robots

insights.claim: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has suggested new jobs will emerge from humans delegating to and supervising robots and AI, but the author argues such advances will not fully compensate for the scope and speed of job displacement, likely eliminating jobs faster than markets and governments can retrain workers, fueling populist and authoritarian alternatives to democracy.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the optimistic 'AI creates new jobs' narrative, arguing the displacement-to-retraining gap itself is a political risk driver worth pricing into social-stability assessments.
insights.locator: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has suggested

insights.claim: A revolution in military affairs is emerging from the synergy of big data, AI, and robotics, layering autonomous battle-management systems that take lethal action faster than humans can monitor with information warfare seeking to corrupt or spoof those same platforms, producing unpredictable and unforeseen outcomes at great cost.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Flags autonomous battle-management and AI-spoofing as an emerging, hard-to-model tail risk for future conflicts, relevant to defense-tech investment and escalation-risk assessment.
insights.locator: In addition to the swarms of autonomous systems

insights.claim: In coming decades the PRC will likely overtake the United States through advances in economic, technological, and military capability, with PRC firms potentially dominating AI via widespread deployment of open-source models and robotics companies such as Unitree and UBTech following the same subsidized-scale playbook already used to dominate renewable energy, EVs, and telecommunications.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explicit prediction of a PRC power transition driven by AI/robotics/quantum dominance, a macro thesis for long-horizon allocation between U.S. and Chinese technology ecosystems.
insights.locator: Fifth, in the coming decades, the PRC will likely overtake

insights.claim: Chinese EVs have captured 85 percent of the market in some Latin American countries, illustrating the same government-subsidized scale-and-cost strategy that is already occurring with Tesla versus BYD, and the U.S. government's recent ban on PRC-built robots from the U.S. market shows Washington is already concerned about the same dynamic spreading to robotics.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: An 85% Chinese EV market share in some Latin American countries is a concrete precedent for how quickly Chinese subsidized-scale strategy can capture emerging-market share in a new technology category.
insights.locator: This is arguably already happening to Tesla vis-à-vis BYD

insights.claim: PRC coercion against Panama over its decision to remove Hong Kong-based Hutchison from two ports illustrates China's growing boldness in the Western Hemisphere, and it is not hard to imagine a confident PRC seeking military bases and formal military cooperation agreements with future anti-U.S. populist regimes in Latin America.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Flags a specific recent incident (Panama-Hutchison) as evidence of rising Chinese assertiveness in the Western Hemisphere, with a forward-looking risk of PRC military basing in the region.
insights.locator: such attitudes are already fueling PRC assertiveness

insights.claim: Growing PRC confidence is likely to lead the Chinese Communist Party to act decisively to end Taiwan's autonomy, potentially timed to assert 'national rejuvenation' ahead of the 2049 centennial of the Communist takeover of the mainland, which would mark a before-and-after moment in China's transition to global dominance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explicitly frames a Taiwan move as a probable, not merely possible, medium-term event tied to a symbolic 2049 deadline — core to any China/Taiwan geopolitical risk model.
insights.locator: Beyond Latin America, that same growing confidence

insights.claim: Nuclear deterrence has been weakened by complacency, China's nuclear buildup, Russian and U.S. abrogation of past treaties such as START, and the expanding number of global nuclear actors, making the chances of a nuclear exchange more likely in the next decade.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explicit warning of rising nuclear-exchange probability driven by treaty erosion and multipolar nuclear buildup, a tail-risk factor for global-order stability.
insights.locator: Nuclear deterrence has been weakened by complacency

insights.claim: A new pandemic could particularly devastate Latin America and the Caribbean, which suffered the highest per-capita death rate from Covid-19, given that international institutions and channels for medical collaboration have been debilitated by distrust and defunding.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Flags degraded global health-cooperation infrastructure as a specific vulnerability for Latin America ahead of any future pandemic shock.
